E001: 'Se come' asks how one eats it – the impersonal 'se' leaves the eater out entirely.

E052: 'O sea' is the everyday in-other-words – it opens the rephrase while the penny drops.
E053: 'Antes de subir' – after a preposition Spanish uses the infinitive, never an -ing form.

E056: 'Siga' and 'doble' show the polite-command swap – -ir verbs end in -a, -ar verbs in -e.

E173: The imperfect paints old states: 'este barrio era mucho más tranquilo' – used to be, no extra verb needed.

V203: 'He comprado' pairs with 'últimamente' – the perfect covers a recent stretch that reaches up to now.
V204: 'Ya se había terminado' – había + participle reaches back before the main past: gone before I got there.
V205: 'Estará' here wonders, not predicts – the future tense is how Spanish muses about a present price.
V206: 'Le pondría' – the conditional floats the idea as what I'd do, a suggestion rather than an instruction.
V207: 'Que no lleve harina' – the recipe is still a wish, not a found thing, so its description goes subjunctive.
V208: After 'si', an unreal condition takes the imperfect subjunctive 'quedara', and 'compraría' gives the result.
V209: 'Por muy poca plata' – 'por' prices the exchange, while 'para toda la semana' marks the stretch covered.
V210: 'Los compro' stays present even with 'desde hace años' – Spanish keeps a still-live habit in the present.
V211: 'Hemos organizado' – haber does the agreeing (hemos = we), while 'organizado' never changes its ending.
V212: 'Ya han llegado' – 'ya' with the perfect announces fresh already-done news that still matters now.
V213: 'Envuelto' is envolver's irregular participle – like 'vuelto' from volver, no 'envolvido' exists.
V214: 'Han pensado' – the perfect suits a have-you-yet question, the deciding may or may not have happened.
V215: 'He encargado' – perfect, not preterite, because the ordering still touches now: the cake awaits pickup.
V216: With 'este año' still running, the perfect fits – 'no hemos tenido tiempo' sits inside an open period.
V217: 'Espero que vengan' – hope offers no guarantee, so the hoped-for verb goes subjunctive: 'vengan', not 'vienen'.
V218: 'Pido que pare' – a request hands the action to someone else, and that hand-over triggers subjunctive 'pare'.
V219: 'Queremos que sea' – when the wanting and the doing belong to different subjects, the verb goes subjunctive.
V220: 'Es mejor que compremos' – a judgement about what should happen sends the verb subjunctive: 'compremos'.
V221: 'No creo que haga falta' – doubt withdraws certainty, so the subjunctive 'haga' replaces plain 'hace'.
V222: 'Me alegra que' runs on emotion, and emotion about a fact still takes subjunctive – 'sirva', not 'sirve'.
V223: 'Si hiciéramos' – the party is only imagined, which is exactly what the imperfect subjunctive flags.
V224: The 'si' half can come last – 'si me avisaran' still takes imperfect subjunctive after 'encantaría'.
V225: 'Pidieron que no subiéramos' – a request made in the past pulls the subjunctive into the past too.
V226: A conditional judgement 'sería bonito que' pushes the next verb to imperfect subjunctive: 'escribiera'.
V227: Events take ser for their when – 'es el sábado en la tarde' – while the venue's location takes 'está'.
V228: 'Elegir el regalo' is the subject of 'me gusta' – a whole infinitive phrase counts as singular.
V229: In the preterite, dar borrows -er/-ir endings – 'dio', one syllable, so no written accent either.
V230: 'Se festejaban' – the imperfect for how things routinely went back then, custom rather than one event.
V231: 'Prendimos' is the one-off preterite event, while 'estaba grabando' paints the action already under way.
V232: 'Ya habían colgado' – habían + participle sets the decorating before another past moment: our arrival.
V233: 'Llegaremos' – the future ending sits on the whole infinitive: llegar + -emos, one word, no will needed.
V234: 'Le importaría' – the conditional softens the ask into would-you-mind, gentler than present 'le importa'.
V235: 'Pasen' and 'dejen' – commands to ustedes borrow the subjunctive form: one plural that covers every guest at once.
V236: 'Para la mesa principal' points at a destination, while 'por si acaso' is a set por phrase: just in case.
V237: 'Se lo damos' – 'les' can't stand before 'lo', so it turns into 'se': se lo, never 'les lo'.
V238: Reporting a question needs 'si' – 'preguntar si el festejo era', with the verb shifted back into the past.
V239: 'Llevamos semanas planeando' – llevar + time + the -ndo form is Spanish's have-been-doing-for pattern.
V240: 'No era para tanto' is the fixed way to say something wasn't worth the worry – 'tanto' stands alone, no noun.
V241: 'Se habrá quedado sin tinta' – habrá + participle makes a confident guess about what already happened.
V242: 'Lo habré dejado' – habré + participle turns the future into a best guess about one's own past doings.
V243: 'Será cosa del bluetooth' – this 'será' guesses about the present, there's no future meaning in it.
V244: 'Tendrá' is a hunch, not a forecast – the future tense doubles as Spanish's way of saying probably.
V245: 'Saldrá muy caro' – asked with the future, the question turns into wondering aloud rather than asking anyone.
V246: 'Se habrá desconectado' – haber's future plus a participle reads as a must-have guess, not a coming event.
V247: 'Se apague' – after 'antes de que' the verb goes subjunctive: the shutdown is a threat, not yet a fact.
V248: 'Para que la música se escuche' – a purpose is an aim, not a fact, so its verb takes subjunctive 'escuche'.
V249: 'Hasta que termine' – the update's end is still pending, so 'termine' goes subjunctive, not 'termina'.
V250: 'En cuanto la cambies' – an as-soon-as pointing at the future takes the subjunctive 'cambies', not 'cambias'.
V251: 'Para que se vea' – after 'para que' Spanish never uses the plain form: the seeing is intended, not achieved.
V252: Question words keep their accent when reported: 'cómo se cambia' – a real asking, no question marks in sight.
V253: 'Me preguntó si la pantalla parpadeaba' – 'si' is whether, turning the question into reported speech.
V254: After 'dijo que' the tense steps back: 'todavía servía' – imperfect for what held true as he spoke.
V255: 'Si este cargador le sirve' stays present – the asking happens now, so nothing pushes the tense back.
V256: 'No supe qué contestar' – a question word straight onto an infinitive: what to answer, no extra verb needed.
V257: 'Es inalámbrico' is what it is, 'está descargado' how it stands – ser and estar split the sentence between them.
V258: 'Me cansa la vista' runs on the 'gustar' pattern – the screen does the tiring, I just receive it.
V259: 'Ayer borré' – 'ayer' dates a finished event, so preterite, and 'me pasé la tarde' is just as closed.
V260: The imperfect 'se mandaban' already means used to – 'antes' sets the era, the tense does the rest.
V261: 'Estaba imprimiendo' has the scene mid-action when 'se quedó' cuts in – interruptions take the preterite.
V262: 'No he revisado el correo todavía' – the perfect for a day still in progress: the checking can still happen.
V263: 'Ya se había arreglado' – the pluperfect for the fix that beat the call: one step further back than 'llamé'.
V264: 'Yo las guardaría' – conditional advice: what I would do in your shoes, gentler than telling you to.
V265: 'Si las instrucciones vinieran' – the unreal if takes imperfect subjunctive, and 'podría' answers with the result.
V266: 'No limpies' – a negative command flips to the -es form, while positive 'busca' keeps its plain shape.
V267: Exchanges take 'por': 'por una portátil' – while 'para llevarla' names what the new machine is for.
V268: 'Se lo adjunté' – Spanish never says le lo: in front of 'lo', the 'le' changes to 'se'.
V269: 'Lleva veinte minutos actualizándose' – 'llevar' + time + gerund: been at it twenty minutes and counting.
V270: 'El cargador que compré' – English may drop that (the charger I bought), the Spanish 'que' never goes.
V271: 'Ya había levantado los puestos' – 'ya' plus pluperfect is the already-too-late pairing: done before 'llegué'.
V272: 'Ya habían cerrado' – plural 'habían' for the unnamed they: whoever locks up had locked up before us.
V273: 'Ya había pasado' – the pluperfect counts back from a past moment, 'cuando saqué el celular', not from now.
V274: 'Había cruzado' – after 'haber' the participle freezes in -o: it never agrees, whoever does the crossing.
V275: 'Ya había zarpado' – 'ya' sits just before the pair: 'había' and its participle travel together, unsplit.
V276: Two layers of past: 'regresamos' is the return, 'había bajado' the shutting that had already beaten it.
V277: After the pluperfect 'ya había pasado', the aftermath sits in the imperfect: 'quedaba' paints the leftovers.
V278: 'Cambió' is the one sharp event, 'íbamos' the crossing already in motion – interruptions take the preterite.
V279: Scene-setters go imperfect: 'había tanto ruido' – then the response, 'nos alejamos', lands in the preterite.
V280: 'Estaba levantada' is a standing state, so imperfect – the one-off answer, 'lo hicimos', takes the preterite.
V281: 'Iba a cruzar' – imperfect 'ir a' means was about to: the crossing was still pending when the car 'giró'.
V282: 'Se veía cerquita' – impressions run in the imperfect, while 'tardamos' logs the fact that proved it wrong.
V283: 'Me fijo' – looking carefully is 'fijarse', the 'me' built in: plain 'fijar' just means to fasten.
V284: 'Me acerco' – to near something is 'acercarse a', reflexive with its preposition included: 'al borde'.
V285: 'Me bajo en la plaza' – plain 'bajar' is to go down, and the 'me' of 'bajarse' makes it getting off.
V286: 'Me canso' – 'cansar' means to tire someone out, and the reflexive turns it inward: I get tired.
V287: 'Los domingos' – a plural article turns the day into a habit: every Sunday, with no word for on.
V288: A story moves in preterites: 'giramos' and 'salimos' – each a completed step that pushes the route on.
V289: 'No he pasado todavía' – the perfect for still-open business: the bridge visit is pending, not history.
V290: 'Habrá algún desvío' – the future used to guess about now: there must be one, going by the traffic.
V291: 'Deberías subir' – 'deber' in the conditional makes should: softer than 'debes', which is you must.
V292: 'Que no sea pura cuesta' – 'sea' goes subjunctive: the path is wished-for, not one anyone has found yet.
V293: 'Sin que uno vaya' – 'sin que' always takes the subjunctive: the guideless visit it names never happens.
V294: 'Apúrese' – the usted command of 'apurarse': pronoun glued on the end, accent keeping the stress put.
V295: 'Para no andar con afán' names the aim, 'por estas calles' the ground covered – purpose against route.
V296: 'Este atajo me lo enseñó' – once the object jumps to the front, 'lo' must repeat it before the verb.
V297: Reporting goes beyond 'dijo': 'me explicó que' works the same, with 'estaba' shifted back into the past.
V298: 'Llevan meses arreglando' – 'llevar' agrees like any verb: plural, because the unnamed they are at it.
V299: 'El que sale al río' – 'el que' is the one that: the article stands in for the alleyway itself.
V300: 'Al final' delivers the verdict – in the end, how it turned out – rather than the end of any street.
